scope_note: Final substantial family backfill for the Hays/Central Texas learner. Integrates existing curated Prunus, Geum and Rubus material, restores missing Rosaceae mappings including Malus, and deliberately broadens the lesson beyond Prunus using drupe, aggregate-drupelet, aggregate-achene and pome fruit architectures.

family_lesson.where_to_look_first: Look for stipules, then inspect the flower for a hypanthium and usually 5 free sepals/5 free petals with several to many stamens. Do not stop there: the decisive next question is fruit architecture—drupe, pome, aggregate drupelets, or aggregate achenes.
family_lesson.strongest_field_confirmation: Usually alternate stipulate leaves + actinomorphic flower + obvious hypanthium/receptacle cup + usually 5 sepals and 5 petals + often numerous free stamens + one to many carpels, followed by highly diagnostic fruit architecture.
core_characters: Leaves usually alternate; simple or compound; margins commonly serrate.
Paired stipules usually present, sometimes conspicuous and sometimes early-caducous.
Hypanthium/receptacular cup usually present and varies from shallow/flat to deep/urn-shaped.
Sepals usually 5 and petals usually 5, but exceptions occur.
Stamens often numerous and inserted around/on the rim of the hypanthium.
Carpels range from one to many, free or fused.
Ovary position ranges from superior to inferior depending on lineage.
Fruit architecture is exceptionally diverse: drupes, pomes, aggregate drupelets, aggregate achenes and more.
avoid_overgeneralizing: Do not teach Rosaceae as 'five petals + many stamens' only; other families can do that too.
Do not teach all Rosaceae ovaries as superior or all as inferior.
Do not assume every family member has persistent obvious stipules; woody taxa may shed them early.
Do not equate Rosaceae with Prunus/drupes; the local pool includes pomes, aggregate drupelets and aggregate achenes.
Do not call a blackberry/dewberry one berry; it is an aggregate fruit made of many drupelets.

hypanthium_lesson.key_point: The hypanthium is the Rosaceae structural thread, but its relationship to the ovary changes across genera.
sequence: Prunus flower side view: shallow cup around a single superior ovary.
Rubus flower: shallow receptacular/hypanthial structure surrounding many free carpels on a raised receptacle.
Geum flower: many free carpels above the receptacle, later becoming many achenes.
Malus/Crataegus flower: hypanthium adnate to the ovary, producing an inferior pome-type fruit.
hypanthium_lesson.caution: Hypanthium presence does not automatically tell you ovary position; teach the ovary-hypanthium relationship per fruit type.

fruit_architecture_key: One fleshy fruit + one hard stone/endocarp -> drupe -> Prunus.
Many tiny fleshy one-seeded units clustered together -> aggregate of drupelets -> Rubus.
Many dry one-seeded achenes on a receptacle, often with persistent styles -> Geum.
Fleshy pome with several carpels forming a central core -> Malus / Crataegus.

genus_anchor_cards.role: single-carpel drupe / classic Rosaceae hypanthium anchor
fastest_cues: Woody tree/shrub with alternate simple often serrate leaves.
Stipules present but often caducous.
Petiolar or marginal glands common in many species.
Five sepals, five petals, many stamens around a cup-shaped hypanthium.
One superior carpel/ovary.
Fruit a drupe with fleshy mesocarp surrounding a single hard stone.

flagship_species.look_here_first: Flowers before leaf-out, coarse doubly serrate leaves, glandular petiole, then a purple-red/blue plum with one flattened stone.
flagship_species.authoritative_note: FNA documents an obconic hypanthium, 5 white petals, hairy leaves, petiolar glands and a 15–30 mm drupe.

fastest_cues: Low trailing/brambling cane.
Recurved prickles common.
Leaves compound/trifoliolate with stipules.
Five petals and many stamens.
Many free carpels, each becoming one tiny drupelet.
Mature fruit is an aggregate drupetum, not a single berry.
genus_anchor_cards.species_detail: FNA describes southern dewberry as frequently creeping, prickly and often glandular-bristly, with black fruits made of about 10–50 coherent drupelets. The torus/receptacle comes away with the ripe fruit, so it is not hollow like a raspberry.

fastest_cues: Herbaceous perennial/short-lived herb rather than woody shrub/tree.
Alternate leaves with stipules; basal and cauline leaves differ.
Five small white petals and many stamens.
Many free carpels.
Fruit an aggregate of dry achenes.
Persistent styles become hooked/jointed on the mature achenes.
genus_anchor_cards.species_detail: FNA describes G. canadense fruiting styles as geniculate-jointed with a persistent proximal segment ending in a hook.

genus_anchor_cards.status: Priority 2 family framework; strict target-zone review pending
fastest_cues: Shrub/tree with short shoots and often stout thorns.
Alternate simple serrate/lobed leaves with stipules.
Corymbose clusters of 5-petaled flowers with many stamens.
Inferior ovary fused/adnate with hypanthium.
Small pome with several hard pyrenes/stone-like units.
genus_anchor_cards.species_detail: FNA describes C. viridis pomes as orange to deep red, usually 5–8 mm, with 3–5 styles/pyrenes in its series.
genus_anchor_cards.teaching_value: Shows that a pome can contain multiple hard pyrene-like units rather than a papery apple-style core.

genus_anchor_cards.status: Priority 3 source concept; strict target-zone review pending
fastest_cues: Woody tree/shrub with alternate simple leaves and stipules.
Five showy petals and many stamens.
Inferior ovary adnate to hypanthium/receptacle.
Pome with fleshy exterior surrounding a multi-carpellate core.
genus_anchor_cards.taxonomy_note: Current POWO accepts Malus ioensis and lists var. texana as a synonym rather than an accepted variety.
genus_anchor_cards.teaching_value: Best fruit-anatomy contrast against Prunus: apple/crabapple pome core versus plum/cherry stone.

fast_key: Stipules + hypanthium + many stamens -> strong Rosaceae signal; then identify fruit type.
Single stone inside fleshy fruit -> Prunus.
Black aggregate fruit made of many drupelets on trailing prickly cane -> Rubus.
Dry burr-like aggregate of hooked achenes on herb -> Geum.
Small thorny tree/shrub + small pome with several hard pyrenes -> Crataegus.
Apple/crabapple-like pome with multi-carpellate core -> Malus.
Many free stamens/carpels but no stipules/hypanthium -> reconsider Ranunculaceae.
Stipulate compound leaves + legume pod -> reconsider Fabaceae.

Ranunculaceae.confusion: Both can have many free stamens and multiple free carpels/achenes.
Ranunculaceae.tie_breaker: Rosaceae usually has stipules and a distinct hypanthium/receptacular cup. Ranunculaceae usually lacks stipules and lacks the characteristic Rosaceae hypanthium; floral-part numbers/forms are often less fixed.

Fabaceae.confusion: Both often have stipules and compound leaves.
Fabaceae.tie_breaker: Fabaceae ultimately gives a legume pod from a single carpel and characteristic papilionoid/mimosoid/caesalpinioid flowers. Rosaceae has a hypanthium and Rosaceae fruit types rather than a legume.

Rhamnaceae.confusion: Woody stipulate plants with small 4–5-part flowers and a floral cup can overlap.
Rhamnaceae.tie_breaker: Rhamnaceae usually has a conspicuous disk and stamens opposite the petals, generally few rather than a many-stamen Rosaceae ring; local Rosaceae fruit architecture is also distinctive.
